comparator.name: Law in Society
comparator.academicYear: 2026-2027 (Teaching and Examination Regulations), first cohort year of the fixed Fall 2026 comparison
comparator.sourceNotes: The current official Teaching and Examination Regulations (OER) 2026-2027 list ten compulsory 6-EC units of education in each of Year 1 and Year 2, plus a compulsory 12-EC Bachelor's thesis and three 6-EC 'Recap' units (Criminal Law, Private Law, Public Law) in Year 3, together with at least 30 EC of elective space in the first semester of Year 3 that a student fills with a VU minor, an Examination-Board-approved equivalent 30-EC package, or exchange credits. The 2025 NVAO accreditation report confirms the programme has no named specialisation or track ('Specialisations or tracks: -'), so no comparator route is selected. The elective minor space is preserved generically at its full 30 EC rather than filled with an invented minor package, since students choose it freely from an open catalogue of VU minors and exchange options. The programme's own marketing and curriculum pages organise the first two years around four recurring themes (security, globalisation of markets, migration, sustainability); those themes are used only to group the OER's compulsory units of education for comparison purposes and do not add or remove any credit-bearing component.
components: Public and Private actors in the Platform Economy
Migration Law and the Nation State

core: Law used as an instrument to analyse and address social challenges, integrating public, private and criminal law around societal problems
Human rights, justice and the philosophical/ethical foundations of law
Combining legal analysis with sociological and psychological perspectives on institutions and behaviour
Empirical legal-social research: quantitative statistics and qualitative methods used to evaluate law and design policy
International law, EU law and global governance, including migration governance
Security, terrorism and criminal justice examined through law, philosophy and psychology
Negotiation, mediation and dispute resolution applied to legal-social problems
adjacent: Sustainability, climate and corporate responsibility, including environmental governance and the ethics of AI/technology
Globalisation of markets, the platform economy and worker/consumer protection
questions: How can law and policy evaluation improve responses to global challenges such as migration, security, sustainability and market globalisation?
How should companies and digital platforms be held accountable for environmental harm and for the treatment of workers and consumers?

alternatives.label: Law, justice and global governance
alternatives.concept: A broad law-and-governance programme combining human rights, criminal, private, constitutional and EU law with international relations, sociology, psychology, philosophy, negotiation and empirical/quantitative and qualitative research methods, reproducing as closely as UCR allows the way Law in Society integrates multiple areas of law with the social sciences to analyse security, criminal justice, international governance and social problems.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum is dominated by doctrinal law (human rights, criminal, private, constitutional, EU and international law) integrated with political science, sociology, psychology, philosophy and negotiation; the combination label describes this multi-field legal/governance programme rather than treating one strand as the whole.
progression: GOSGATE102 (the shared law gateway) and other level-1 foundations (GOSLAWJ111, GOSSOCI111, BENGATE102, BENGATE101, HCBPSYC111) precede the level-2/3 GOSLAWJ criminal, private, constitutional and EU law courses and BENBUSI311/BENLEAD312, which in turn precede the level-3 capstone courses (GOSPOLI311, GOSPOLI313, GOSLAWJ312, ENSDELT312) in Year 3; all formal prerequisites are completed in an earlier semester and every course is scheduled in a semester in which it is offered.

alternatives.label: Sustainability, business and global-markets governance
alternatives.concept: A business, economics and environmental-governance programme examining how law, regulation and corporate practice should respond to the globalisation of markets, the platform economy and climate/sustainability responsibility, reorganising the evidenced sustainability and globalisation-of-markets themes around business, economics and environmental-governance coursework rather than doctrinal law.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum is dominated by business, economics and sustainability-governance courses (international business, public economics, econometrics, market research, marketing, sustainability essentials, governance of sustainability, applied sustainability research) with only a small doctrinal-law and human-rights anchor, so the sustainability/business/markets label accurately describes the completed programme rather than its law origin.
alternatives.distinctness: This route replaces 15 of the 24 courses used in the closest-match programme (all of the criminal, constitutional and EU-law courses, political theory, peace & conflict, negotiation, philosophy, extremism and most social-science courses) with business, economics and environmental-governance coursework (international business and governance, public economics, econometrics, marketing, market research, sustainability essentials I/II, life-cycle analysis, applied sustainability research, and data science). It keeps only a minimal shared anchor (PPD, the transnational business-law course, the two business/research gateways, human-rights law, AI ethics, climate change and sustainability governance) and organises the whole curriculum around corporate and market accountability rather than around doctrinal criminal, constitutional and international law.
progression: BENGATE101, BENGATE102 and ENSGATE101 (the business, research-methods and sustainability gateways) are scheduled in Year 1 and precede every course that requires them (BENBUSI311, BENENTR211/212/311/312, BENECON211/211/312, ENSGATE201); ENSGATE101 also precedes ENSGATE201. All other courses have no formal prerequisite. Foundational Year 1 sustainability, business and law content precedes the Year 2-3 applied and quantitative courses, and every course is scheduled in a semester in which it is offered.

candidates.label: Sustainability, corporate accountability and global markets

selection.assessment: The closest-match programme covers the core law-and-justice field together with the security and international-governance stable directions (migration/refugee law and security/terrorism are substantively covered by its criminal, international and human-rights law content, since UCR offers no dedicated migration-law course). The sustainability/globalisation-of-markets direction is evidenced by two further stable study directions and three direct interests and organises a genuinely distinct 24-course business/economics/environmental-governance programme, differing from the closest match by 15 of 24 courses. Every generator-eligible interest row is now owned by one of these two programmes, leaving no remaining coherent, evidence-backed direction for a third alternative; production stops at two.

blocks: Security, criminal justice and legal philosophy
Both examine the criminal-justice system's response to harmful behaviour; VU's Criminology unit is taught within the LiS law-in-society framing UCR's Criminal Law & Criminal Justice course also uses.
The selected UCR programmes do not include a course that directly reproduces defamation and assault liability; related private-law liability content, where present, is distributed elsewhere.
The selected UCR programmes do not include a course that directly reproduces this diversity component; related social-psychology content, where present, is distributed elsewhere.
Both are introductory empirical-research-methods courses teaching research design and statistics.
Both combine legal philosophy with substantive legal analysis; VU applies this combination to security while UCR applies it to human rights.
Both are introductory psychology courses; UCR's course specifically covers social psychology.
Both examine the drivers of terrorism and political violence; UCR's course focuses on radicalisation and extremism specifically.
Globalisation of markets and business law
Both examine multinational business conduct and its governance across borders.
Both examine the legal regulation of platform and multinational business actors; UCR's course frames this as transnational business law.
Both are quantitative-methods courses; UCR's econometrics course extends statistics to economic evidence.
Migration, qualitative methods and dispute resolution
Both examine the international-law framework within which migration is governed; UCR's course covers public international law generally rather than migration specifically.

The selected UCR programmes do not include a course that directly reproduces migration law and the nation-state; UCR offers no dedicated migration-law course, so related international and human-rights law content, where present, is distributed elsewhere.
Both teach qualitative interviewing and interpretive research methods.
Both teach negotiation, mediation and dispute-resolution skills.
Sustainability, technology ethics and applied evaluation research
Both examine artificial intelligence; UCR's course focuses specifically on its ethical implications.
Both are applied, project-based empirical research/evaluation courses; UCR's applies the method to a sustainability problem rather than to legal-policy evaluation.
Both examine the governance and ethics of sustainability.
Both examine local environmental-justice and social-movement claims about sustainability, paralleling VU's Amsterdam case study.
Personal development, private/public-law recap, thesis and elective space
Both are private-law courses; VU's is an advanced third-year review of principles UCR's course introduces directly.
Both examine constitutional/public law; VU's is an advanced third-year review while UCR's course introduces comparative constitutional law directly.

The selected UCR programmes include only one criminal-law course (matched above to VU's first-year Criminology unit); UCR offers no second, more advanced criminal-law course to match this third-year recap.

notes.text: Law in Society requires ten compulsory law/social-science units in each of Year 1 and Year 2, a 12-EC bachelor's thesis and three advanced 'Recap' law courses reviewing criminal, private and public law in Year 3. UCR's selected programmes can combine a comparable range of law, social-science and (in the second alternative) business/sustainability courses, but neither reproduces VU's dedicated migration-law course, its second criminal-law unit, or its compulsory bachelor's thesis; UCR's standardized Optional independent research element is offered instead of a required thesis.
